title: Practice Test 1: Local food shops
instructions: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Hi Shannon – how are you settling into your new flat?

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Really well, thanks.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: You look like you’re going shopping.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Yes, I am. My cousins are coming to stay for a couple of days, and I have to cook for them.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Well, there are plenty of places to buy food in Kite Place – it’s the area by the harbour.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Oh, OK, I’ll find that on the map. Thanks.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: What sort of food do you need to get?

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Well, neither of them eats meat but they both like fish.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Well, there’s a really good fish market there.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Oh great – where is it exactly?

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: It’s at the far end of Kite Place, so you have to go over the bridge and then it’s on the right.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: OK – is it open all day?

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: It doesn’t close until four, but I’d recommend going earlier than that – it does run out of some things.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Oh, I don’t want that to happen.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: As long as you get there by 3.30, you should be fine. It’s only 11 now, so plenty of time.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Do you need to buy vegetables too?

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: I do, and I want to avoid all the plastic packaging in the supermarket!

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Well, there’s a really nice organic shop there. Now what’s it called . . . it’s the name of a flower. I know, it’s ‘Rose’.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: That’s a nice name.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Yeah – it sells vegetables and quite a lot of other stuff.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: And where’s that?

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Well, as you reach the market, you’ll see a big grey building on your left – I think it used to be a warehouse. Anyway, now it’s a restaurant upstairs, but the ground floor has two shops either side of the entrance and it’s the one on the left.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: That’s easy enough.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: You can’t miss it – there’s also a big sign on the pavement so you can look for that.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Fine! I guess if I need anything else, I’ll have to go to the supermarket.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Yeah – you should be able to get everything you need, but there’s a minibus that goes to the supermarket if you need it. It’s purple and the number is 289.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Thanks, that’s great.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: So what do you need to get at the fish market? The salmon is always very good and the shellfish.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: I’m going to make a curry, I think, and I need about 12 prawns for that.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: They’ll have plenty of those.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: OK.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Have you ever tried samphire?

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: No – what’s that?

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: It’s a type of seaweed. I just ask for a handful and you fry it in butter. It’s delicious!

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Oh, I might try that – how do you spell it?

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: It’s S-A-M-P-H-I-R-E.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Great – it’s always good to try something different.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: I’ll see what beans they have in the organic shop and I think I’ll get something for dessert there.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: How about a mango?

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: I’m not sure – they’re not always ripe. I’d prefer a melon – it’s bigger too.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Good idea. The owner also sells a lot of spices there that you can put in a curry, and things like coconut.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Oh, that’s very helpful. I’ll have a look.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: No problem.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: I know bread doesn’t really go with curry but I always like to have some in case.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: As I said – all the bread is home-made and there’s lots of variety. I like the brown bread myself.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Mm, sounds good.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: They sell other things there too.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Like cakes? I love chocolate cake.

lines.speaker: Leon
lines.text: Well – not that, but they have a whole range of tarts and the best are the strawberry ones.

lines.speaker: Shannon
lines.text: Perfect – hopefully I won’t even have to go to the supermarket!

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: The children’s book festival is coming up again soon and here to tell us all about it is the festival’s organiser, Jenny Morgan. So tell us what we can expect this year, Jenny.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: Well, as usual we’ve got five days of action-packed exciting events for children, with writers coming from all over the country getting involved. Just to give you an idea of what’s on offer in the workshops, first of all, there’s a very special event called Superheroes. This is a chance for deaf children to share their reading experiences with author Madeleine Gordon, who is herself hearing impaired.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: ‘Just do it’ is a practical workshop led by the well-known illustrator Mark Keane. He’ll take participants on a magical journey to faraway lands with an opportunity for aspiring actors to do some role play.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: ‘Count on me’ is an inspiring and entertaining look at the issues of friendship for 13–14-year-olds. It looks at some of the friendships described in popular books and asks participants to compare these with their own experiences.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: ‘Speak up’ is part of a series of workshops on the subject of mental health. This is a creative writing workshop encouraging children to describe situations where young people experience loneliness. A recent survey revealed that children can be lonely even when they’re at home with their families.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: ‘Jump for joy’, as many of you will know, is the heart-warming, best-selling story by Nina Karan about a young girl’s trip to visit her relatives in India. It recently received the gold medal at the Waterford Awards. Nina will get children to celebrate the word ‘joy’ by writing a poem.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: ‘Sticks and stones’ is the beautifully illustrated picture book for young readers about a community who organise an African-Caribbean festival to help local children learn about their Jamaican roots. This will be a musical event where children will have the chance to play steel drums. This is bound to be very popular, so please book as soon as possible.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Thanks Jenny. That all sounds really interesting. I’m just wondering if you have a favourite book you could recommend for our readers?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: It’s hard to choose, but Alive and Kicking is definitely worth mentioning. You won’t have heard of the writer as it’s her first book – which is really impressive. It’s basically the teenage diary of a boy from Somalia who comes to live in the UK. It deals with the serious issue of immigration and all the challenges the boy has to face at school and with the language barrier, etc. Usually, books like this are quite sad, but this one actually made me cry with laughter. On each page, there are simple but hilarious black and white stick drawings of the boy with his friends and teachers. At the end of each diary entry, there are new English words the boy learns each day, which may help develop some children’s vocabulary.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: I think my kids would enjoy that. What about any advice for parents on how to encourage their children to read more?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: Well, this is something I get asked about a lot. There are so many distractions for kids these days that it can be hard to find time for reading. One thing I’d say is to make time to sit down with your child and share books with them. A lot of parents give up reading aloud to their children as soon as they learn to read independently, but this is a mistake. It’s good to read more advanced books to them as it helps to develop their vocabulary. If you don’t have time for this, then let them listen to audio books. Often, they’ll want to read books they’ve listened to for themselves. I think it’s a good idea to make a mental note of the type of books your child is reading – often they just read the same genre all the time, which can get a bit boring. You can introduce new authors and genres to them. Librarians should be able to help you with this.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Well Jenny, I think that’s really useful. . . .

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Hi Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: It’s harder than I expected, but I’ve got some great classes. How about you?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Not brilliant. I’m really struggling with my Year 12 science class.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Are they hard to control?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Well, I don’t have discipline problems as such. It’s just that they don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It’s depressing. They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren’t too bad, but there’s no real engagement.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do. I was wondering about something on the children’s diets . . . you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Mmm. Let’s think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat. OK, but you’d also need to have access to the children’s medical records and I don’t think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue. If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it’s not going to be easy.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Wouldn’t that be upsetting for the children?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Well, the animals don’t have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they’re given a certain diet and the effects are observed.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Yes, you’d have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it’s quite straightforward.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn’t necessarily be true for people, would it?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: No that’s true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It’s inevitable.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Yes. You’d need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements . . . things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Mmm. That might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don’t really need?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable. Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don’t do much.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . . or use mice with a different genetic structure. But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Sure. I did a similar experiment in college actually.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Great. So how many mice would I need?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: I’d say about 12. And all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: OK. And I’d need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group. And how would I tell them apart? I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group . . . or just mark them in some way?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: You could use food colouring, that wouldn’t hurt them.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: Perfect. Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let’s call them group A, would be the control group. So they’d just have ordinary mouse food. I suppose you can buy that?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they’d also have the extra sugar.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Would you just give them straight sugar?

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: It might be better to give them something like cereal with it.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Mmm. Then you’d need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week. And you’d need an electronic balance.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: But we can’t hold them on the balance, or it’d affect the reading.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Exactly. So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away. It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.

lines.speaker: Clare
lines.text: OK. So once we’ve measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation. And then see where we go from there. That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Yes. One thing . . .

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to be talking about microplastics. Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres in size. Recently there's been a greater awareness that there are large quantities of plastic waste – big and small – in the environment. The amount of plastic waste in the oceans has received widespread attention, but far less is known about the effects of microplastics in freshwater and particularly in soil.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Microplastics can enter the environment via a number of different sources. Threads and microfibres detach from synthetic clothing every time they're put in a washing machine, and these find their way into the water system. Other sources include big pieces of plastic waste that are already in the environment, and these break down into microscopic particles over a period of time. On a larger scale, factory waste is another route, as are tyres which wear down as cars, lorries and so on travel along road surfaces.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: We already understand some of the impacts of microplastics from studies involving fish and other animals. There is evidence that microplastics harm small creatures in a variety of ways, such as by damaging their mouths, or by impairing their ability to feed, for example when microplastics get lodged in their digestive system.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Surprisingly perhaps, it is likely that humans consume microplastics, as these have been detected in a wide range of food and drink products, including bottled water, as well as in water that comes direct from the tap. What's more, salt and many kinds of seafood have also been found to contain microplastics.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: However, it's important to underline that there is not yet conclusive proof that microplastics cause significant harm to people. In many countries, including here in the UK, there is legislation which prevents manufacturers from adding plastic microbeads to shower gels, facial cleansers and toothpaste.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: It is very difficult to accurately estimate the total amount of microplastic particles in the soil as they can be hard to detect, but we do know they are carried in the air and deposited in the soil by rain. What's more, many of the fertilisers used by both farmers and gardeners contain microplastics.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: A team from the Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge has carried out a study of the effects of microplastics on the digestive tracts of earthworms. These worms, which live in topsoil, are an essential component of our agricultural system. By feeding on soil, they mix nutrients into it, thereby making it more fertile.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The researchers set out to discover whether the introduction of microplastics into the soil – and the subsequent ingestion of these by earthworms – would impact soil quality and ultimately inhibit plant growth. The short answer was, yes, it did. After placing three different types of microplastic particles into the soil, they planted perennial rye grass. The particles of microplastic, which included biodegradable PLA and conventional high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, were then ingested by the earthworms in the soil. The result was that the worms lost weight rapidly. What's more, a lower percentage than normal of the rye grass seeds germinated, and the researchers concluded that this was a direct result of the earthworms being unable to fulfil their normal role in making soil more fertile. The team also discovered that there was an increase in the amount of acid found in the soil, and this was attributed mainly to the microplastic particles from conventional HDPE plastic.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The conclusions of the study make for very interesting reading – I've included the reference in the notes to give you at the end of this session. To summarise, the authors proposed the idea that we need to regard soil as we would regard any other process in nature. This means we should accept the implications of soil being dependent on decaying and dead matter constantly being passed through the bodies of earthworms. That is, when soil becomes impoverished by the presence of microplastics, not only ecosystems but also the whole of society are negatively impacted.
